Bi.title: How bias gets in, and how it can grow
Bi.caption: Bias usually starts in the data: a model copies the patterns in past decisions, including unfair ones. If its own decisions are fed back in as new data, the gap can grow. Made-up numbers.

Fa.title: Fair by which measure?
Fa.caption: Fairness has more than one definition, and they can't always all be met at once. A tool can look equally accurate for two groups while its mistakes land much harder on one of them, so each group is checked on the measure that matters for the decision. Made-up numbers.

Xa.title: Two kinds of explanation
Xa.caption: Explainability tools, such as SHAP and LIME, estimate which inputs mattered: for the model as a whole (global) or for one answer (local). They're approximations of what the model does, not a full account of it. Made-up numbers.

Tn.title: What being open about AI covers
Tn.caption: Transparency means telling people that AI is being used, what it was built from, where it fails and who is responsible. A model card is one common way to write this down. In the EU, the AI Act has required telling people and labelling AI-generated content since August 2026.

Pv.title: Where your words go, and what to ask
Pv.caption: Each step is a place to ask what happens to your data. Under the UK GDPR, organisations should collect only what they need, keep it secure, keep it no longer than necessary and explain how it is used.

Rs.title: Responsible AI, step by step
Rs.caption: Responsible AI turns principles into checks at every stage, from deciding whether to build something at all to watching it after launch, when new problems often appear.

Et.title: Who gains, who could be harmed?
Et.caption: Ethics weighs who gains and who could be harmed, and whether people agreed to it. Reasonable people can weigh these differently, which is why it's discussed, not calculated.

An.title: Hitting the target, missing the point
An.caption: AI is trained on something measurable that stands in for what we really want. When the two drift apart, the model can hit the target and miss the point: researchers call this specification gaming. Flattering people, sycophancy, is one result that has been linked to training on human ratings.

Rt.title: The red-team loop
Rt.caption: Red teams try to break a model before the public does. Every failure they find becomes a fix, and a new test so it stays fixed. Red teaming finds problems; it can't prove a model is safe.

Wm.title: How a text watermark can work
Wm.caption: One research method (Kirchenbauer and others, 2023): before each word, a secret key splits the possible next words into green and red halves, and the model is nudged towards green. A detector with the key counts them. Heavy rewording weakens the signal, so it's evidence, not proof. Made-up example.

Sf.title: Two kinds of harm, many layers
Sf.caption: AI safety covers accidents (the AI gets something harmfully wrong) and misuse (someone uses it to do harm). No single layer catches everything, so safety teams stack several, before and after release.

Dg.title: Rules for data, from start to finish
Dg.caption: Data governance means agreed rules for every stage of data's life, and named people responsible for them. In a school, that decides who can see pupil data, and whether an AI tool may.

Re.title: Same AI, different rules, depending on use
Re.caption: The EU AI Act sets rules by use, not by technology. Its bans have applied since February 2025 and its transparency rules since August 2026; dates for high-risk rules have been under review. The UK has no single AI law and relies mainly on existing laws, such as data protection and equality law.

Ip.title: Two copyright questions
Ip.caption: In the UK, text and data mining of others' work is clearly allowed only for non-commercial research (section 29A of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988); in 2026 the government dropped a proposed broad exception for AI training. Ownership of AI-made work is still being settled.

Aw.title: Three questions for an "AI-powered" claim
Aw.caption: AI washing is overclaiming AI to ride the hype. Regulators have acted: in March 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission fined two investment firms for AI claims they could not back up.

Sh.title: Approved tool or shadow AI?
Sh.caption: Shadow AI is using AI tools that haven't been approved. The risk is less the tool itself than what happens to the data, and that nobody responsible knows it's being used.

Hp.title: Where the extra value comes from
Hp.caption: The human premium rests on proof as much as on the object: people pay more when they can trust a person made it. Records of the making and verified labels, such as Content Credentials, provide that proof.

Rv.title: Two ways into an AI model
Rv.caption: Reverse engineering an AI model means probing it from outside (inputs and outputs) or, when its weights are available, studying it from inside. Probing a closed service may break its terms of use.

Mp.title: Finding the ideas inside a model
Mp.caption: Mechanistic interpretability looks inside a model to find which parts carry which ideas. In 2024, Anthropic found millions of such features in a production model using sparse autoencoders, and checked them by turning them up and down. It's still far from a complete map.

As.title: Steering a reply without retraining
As.caption: Activation steering finds a direction inside the model by comparing contrasting prompts, then adds it while the model answers. It changes this reply, not the model itself, and too much can make replies strange.

Mx.title: Copying a model through its answers
Mx.caption: Model extraction copies a model's behaviour, not its files. Researchers showed in 2016 that prediction services could be copied this way. It usually breaks the service's terms and may break the law.

Rd.title: One direction that means "refuse"
Rd.caption: In 2024 researchers found that, across 13 open chat models, refusing harmful requests runs through a single direction in the model's internal numbers. It shows how much safety can hang on one small part of a model.

Ab.title: Removing a model's "no"
Ab.caption: Abliteration builds on the refusal direction: removing it from an open model's weights stops the model refusing. That only removes a safety behaviour; it doesn't make harmful or illegal content legal.

Uc.title: How an uncensored model differs from a jailbreak
Uc.caption: An uncensored model has its refusals removed from the file itself, unlike a jailbreak, which tricks an unchanged model. Because it runs on someone's own computer, nobody can patch it. Illegal content is still illegal, whichever tool makes it.

Su.title: Learn from answers, then test on new ones
Su.caption: Supervised learning trains on examples that come with the right answers. The honest test is on examples kept back from training: a model can score well on what it has seen and badly on what it hasn't. Made-up numbers.

Un.title: Finding groups no one named
Un.caption: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data with no answers attached. It can find the groups, but people still decide what each group means, and whether it is useful.

Rr.title: Choosing the line with the smallest errors
Rr.caption: Regression finds the line (or curve) that keeps the errors, the gaps between real points and the line, as small as possible overall. Its predictions are best read as a likely range. Made-up numbers.

Cl.title: Where to draw the line
Cl.caption: Most classifiers give a score, and a threshold turns it into a decision. Moving the threshold trades one mistake for another, so the right setting depends on which mistake matters more. Made-up example.

Cu.title: How k-means finds groups
Cu.caption: K-means, one common clustering method, repeats two steps, assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the middle of its points, until nothing changes. You choose how many groups it looks for.

Dt.title: How a tree picks its questions
Dt.caption: A decision tree is built by trying possible questions and keeping the one that best separates the answers into pure groups, then repeating inside each branch. Made-up data.

Rf.title: Why a forest of trees differs
Rf.caption: A random forest gives each tree a different random sample of the rows and of the questions it may ask. Different trees make different mistakes, so the vote is steadier than any one tree.

Gb.title: Each model learns what is left over
Gb.caption: Gradient boosting adds small models one at a time, each trained on the errors still left. It is one of the most accurate methods for tables of data. Made-up numbers.

Fe.title: Three ways to make better features
Fe.caption: Models only see numbers, and they learn faster from numbers that capture what matters. Combining, transforming and encoding raw data are three common ways to make better features. Made-up example.

Of.title: The sweet spot between too simple and too complex
Of.caption: Overfitting shows up as a gap: training error keeps falling while error on new data starts rising. Checking on kept-back data shows where to stop.

Ad.title: Learn what is normal, flag what is far from it
Ad.caption: Anomaly detection learns a picture of normal and scores how far each new event is from it. Flags are for a person to check: unusual isn't always wrong. Made-up example.

Fc.title: A forecast is a range, not a point
Fc.caption: Good forecasts come with a range. The further ahead they look, the wider it gets: next week is easier to predict than next term. Made-up numbers.

Tm.title: Trend, season and the rest
Tm.caption: Time-series methods often split data into a trend, a repeating season and leftover noise. A jump that is just "summer again" isn't news; a change in the trend might be. Made-up data.

Pa.title: From what happened to what will happen
Pa.caption: Predictive analytics turns past data into a likely future, stated with how sure it is. It is the third of four common analytics steps, before deciding what to do. Made-up numbers.

Ps.title: Compare the options, then recommend one
Ps.caption: Prescriptive analytics goes one step past prediction: it tests the options against the forecast and the constraints, and recommends one. People still make the call. Made-up example.

Rc.title: Two ways to recommend
Rc.caption: Recommenders suggest things like what you liked, and things people like you liked. Every click feeds back in, so a feed can narrow over time unless it mixes in something new.

Ch.title: From a risk score to an action
Ch.caption: Churn prediction is only useful if it leads to action, and if that action is tested: compared with similar customers who got nothing, did it change anything? Made-up numbers.

Sa.title: Why tone is hard to read
Sa.caption: Sentiment analysis works well on clear reviews and struggles with sarcasm, negation and mixed opinions. Scoring each topic separately, such as food and service, gives a truer picture.

Np.title: From words to an action
Np.caption: Language processing turns messy human words into something a computer can act on: what you want (the intent) and the details. Today's large language models handle several of these steps in one go.

Cv.title: What a computer sees in a picture
Cv.caption: Computer vision starts from numbers, one per pixel, and builds up from edges to shapes to objects. Like any model, it can be fooled by things it rarely saw in training, such as unusual lighting.

Ge.title: How an AI answer chooses its sources
Ge.caption: Generative engine optimisation tries to get pages cited in AI answers. One study (Aggarwal and others, 2024) found adding citations, quotations and statistics helped most, but results vary and added numbers still need to be true.

Ga.title: Analysing versus creating
Ga.caption: Generative AI learns patterns from huge numbers of examples, then produces new text, images, audio, video or code that fit them. The output is what is likely, not what is checked.

Mm.title: Different inputs, one shared model
Mm.caption: Multimodal models turn text, images and sound into the same kind of numbers, so one model can read them together, and some can answer in more than one mode too.

Df.title: Add noise to learn; remove it to create
Df.caption: A diffusion model learns by watching pictures dissolve into noise and practising the reverse. To make a new picture, it starts from noise and cleans it up in many small steps, steered by the prompt.

Gn.title: A forger and a detective
Gn.caption: A GAN trains a generator and a discriminator against each other. When the discriminator can only guess, right about half the time, the fakes are realistic. Diffusion models have since overtaken GANs for most image tools. Made-up numbers.

Ti.title: What you asked, and what the tool decided
Ti.caption: Text-to-image tools fill every gap in your prompt with their own defaults, learned from training images. Say what matters, then check what it decided for you.

Ts.title: From text to a voice
Ts.caption: Modern text-to-speech sounds natural because a neural model learned from hours of recorded speech. Voice cloning can copy a person from a short sample: only use a voice with that person's permission.

Ft.title: A short extra course for one job
Ft.caption: Fine-tuning changes a trained model's settings with a small, focused set of examples. It is far cheaper than starting again, but the examples must be good, and other skills can slip. Made-up numbers.

Fs.title: Examples in the prompt, not new training
Fs.caption: Few-shot prompting shows the model a few examples so it copies the pattern. Zero-shot gives none, one-shot gives one. Unlike fine-tuning, the model itself doesn't change.

Rm.title: Thinking before answering
Rm.caption: Reasoning models are trained to work through a problem, and check their steps, before answering. They do better at maths, coding and logic, but are slower and cost more, and their steps can still go wrong.

Sd.title: Useful extra data, with a catch
Sd.caption: Synthetic data fills gaps and protects privacy. A 2024 Nature study (Shumailov and others) showed that models trained over and over on generated data lose the rare cases first, so real data must stay in the mix.

Dk.title: Stop, check the source, report
Dk.caption: Deepfakes are getting too good to spot by eye, so check the source, not just the pixels. In England and Wales, creating a sexual deepfake of an adult without consent has been a crime since 6 February 2026; any sexual image of an under-18 is illegal. Young people can use Childline's Report Remove.

Vc.title: The loop that skips the checks
Vc.caption: Vibe coding is great for quick prototypes and learning. Before real users or real data, someone has to read, test and security-check the code: Veracode (2025) found flaws in 45% of AI-written samples.

Ce.title: Everything the model reads, not just your question
Ce.caption: Context engineering decides what the model gets to read: rules, documents, examples, tool results, memory and the question. The window has a limit, so choosing what to leave out matters as much as what to put in.

Gv.title: Every frame has to agree
Gv.caption: Generative video makes many frames that must agree with each other. Today's tools make short clips and still slip on physics, hands and text, and most label or watermark what they make.

Sp.title: Cheap to make, costly to sort through
Sp.caption: AI slop spreads because it costs almost nothing to make and clicks still pay. It drowns out real work and can mislead. Check for a named source, and don't feed it with shares.

2d.title: AI suggests, the designer decides
2d.caption: AI tools can produce lots of 2D ideas quickly. A designer still chooses, edits and checks them, and a laser cutter needs vector paths, not a pixel picture.

3d.title: Set the goals, let it propose shapes
3d.caption: In 3D design, AI-driven generative design proposes shapes that meet set goals and limits. People set the goals and must still check and test the result, because a design that passes on screen can fail in use.

Rp.title: A bot that copies your clicks
Rp.caption: RPA bots follow the same clicks and typing every time. They are fast and tireless on fixed steps, but brittle: a changed screen or an unusual email breaks them.

Ia.title: Bots plus AI that can decide
Ia.caption: Intelligent automation lets bots handle work that needs judgement, like sorting messages, by adding AI. Low-confidence cases should go to a person. Made-up numbers.

Hy.title: Many tools, one process
Hy.caption: Hyperautomation, a term Gartner popularised in 2019, means combining many automation and AI tools across whole processes. Not every step should be automated: people keep the judgement calls.

Tg.title: What starts an automation
Tg.caption: Trigger, condition, action: the shape of almost every automation. A badly chosen trigger can fire too often, or never, so test it.

En.title: Act the moment it happens
En.caption: Event-driven automations react as things happen instead of checking on a timer. That is faster and wastes fewer checks, but the system sending the events has to be reliable.

Wh.title: A message sent the moment something happens
Wh.caption: A webhook is one app calling another's web address the moment something happens, with the details attached. Because anyone could send to that address, the receiver should check a signature.

Lc.title: Build it from blocks
Lc.caption: Low-code and no-code tools let non-programmers build apps and automations quickly. The questions don't go away: whose data does it touch, who maintains it, and what happens when it breaks?

Id.title: From a pile of paper to checked data
Id.caption: IDP combines OCR, classification and extraction. The confidence score decides what flows through and what a person checks. Made-up example.

Oc.title: From pixels to letters
Oc.caption: OCR turns pictures of text into text a computer can search and edit. It is very accurate on clear print, less so on handwriting or poor photos, so important numbers are worth a check.

Mi.title: How the work really flows
Mi.caption: Process mining uses event logs, which case, which step, when, to map how work really flows, including loops and waits nobody planned. Made-up numbers.

Be.title: Rules people write, applied the same way every time
Be.caption: Rules engines are predictable and easy to explain, unlike models that learn from data. But they only know the cases someone thought of, so unusual cases need a person.

St.title: Straight through, or out to a person
St.caption: Straight-through processing removes hand-offs, so routine jobs finish in seconds. The checks along the way, and a clear route out for exceptions, are what make it safe. Made-up numbers.

Dw.title: What is inside a "digital worker"
Dw.caption: "Digital worker" is a marketing name for a bundle of bots, AI and rules. It can save time, but it is not a colleague: a person owns its work, its access and its mistakes.

Va.title: From "Hey…" to a reminder
Va.caption: Virtual assistants turn speech into actions on your phone or speaker. A chatbot is mainly for conversation; a copilot sits inside one app. All of them can mishear, so check important ones.

Cp.title: It suggests; you decide
Cp.caption: Copilots speed up drafting by suggesting as you work. In one controlled study (Peng and others, 2023) developers finished a coding task 55.8% faster. Checking what you accept is still your job.
